$doc: The slide-in panel's appearance, as data — the source of the `@component drawer` block in css/components.css and of dist/react/drawer.tsx. THE INTERESTING HALF IS THE LAST THIRD, and it is the reason this block reads as a candidate for the census's `foreign-selector` and is not one: nine of its rules are about components the drawer HOSTS rather than owns — `.drawer .chat`, `.drawer .idx__row`, `.drawer .entry`, `.drawer .profile` — and every one of them is the scoped part `section-head` already forced, `within` naming a rule this definition declares and the target being one class that belongs to somebody else. The coupling is recorded rather than hidden: it lands in dist/components.json's class list for `drawer`, because that file parses the shipped CSS. Two constructs are new here. A `contains` may hold NOTHING (`:empty`), which is what an element's contents are called when there are none. And a part may be a SCOPE with no declarations of its own — `.drawer .profile > div` is not a rule the stylesheet writes, it is the wrapper whose odd children carry the gutter, and emitting it empty would claim a rule the file has not got.

block.title: Drawer (slide-in panel)
note: A right-hand panel that slides over the page, with a scrim behind it. It
HOSTS a surface; it is not one. Everything about a conversation still
belongs to Chat — the drawer contributes a frame, a portrait, a title and a
way out, and knows nothing else about what is inside it.
WHY THIS IS NOT A CHAT VARIANT, since that was the cheaper option. The
first sentence of components/chat/spec.md is that chat "is a section of the
page, not a widget floating over it — it lives inside a `.band`/`.well` and
obeys the skeleton's rules like everything else." A `position: fixed` rule
inside the chat block would make that sentence false, and `@component`
ownership is per BLOCK, so dist/components.json would then report `chat` as
owning a scrim and a z-index. The drawer is also not chat-shaped: it is the
generic answer to "summon a surface from anywhere", and the moment a second
thing wants that (a filter panel, a source inspector) a chat variant would
have to be renamed anyway.
THE DRAWER IS PRESENTATION ONLY. JS toggles exactly one attribute —
`data-open` on `.drawer` — and never writes a style. Everything below reads
off that attribute, which is why the open/close animation, the a11y-tree
removal and the tab-order removal cannot disagree with each other.
Over the bar (100), under the case dialog (500): an answer in the drawer
renders real `.idx__row`s that call `window.openCase`, and the case study
must land on top of the drawer that opened it, not behind it.
`visibility`, not `display`, is what closes this. It removes the panel
from the tab order and the accessibility tree exactly as `display: none`
does, but it is animatable — so the delay below lets the sheet finish
sliding out before the layer stops existing. A JS-set `hidden` attribute
would cut the close animation off at frame one.

rules.name: open
rules.$doc: The one attribute js/drawer.js writes. Everything visible about an open drawer is scoped to it — the scrim's opacity and the sheet's transform are both parts declared `within` this state, which is the shape only a NAMED reference can reach: `.drawer[data-open]` owns no selector of its own for an author to quote.

rules.name: sheet
note: THE WIDTH IS A READING MEASURE, not a proportion of the window. The
assistant's answers were arriving in a 431px column and were called
unreadable; 46rem (736px) less the body's inset leaves a 696px reading
column, and `.chat__prose`'s own 44rem cap then does the rest — measured at
1280px, the prose sets 619px wide, which is NARROWER than the same paragraph
on the page. It is also close to the page's own content column (887px at a
1080px viewport), which is what lets an answer render as the site's real
components instead of a narrow imitation of them.
Below 1024px the drawer becomes the whole screen. That is not a fallback:
at 1024 a 736px panel leaves a 288px sliver of page, which reads as a
mistake rather than as context, and every component the answer renders
already has its own narrow layout at that width. `100%` rather than `100vw`
on purpose — `100vw` counts the scrollbar and would overhang by its width in
the moment before the body scroll lock takes effect.
Both tracks are `minmax(0, …)` and that is load-bearing, not defensive.
A grid track's automatic minimum is min-content, so ONE unbreakable
display-cased project name inside an answer sizes the column, the column
sizes the sheet, and the sheet overflows a panel with an explicit width.
Measured at 375px before this: the head's Close button was pushed off the
screen and every turn ran past the right edge. Same failure, and same
fix, as `.sec__title { min-width: 0 }`.

rules.name: portrait
note: THE PORTRAIT CARRIES ITS OWN GROUND, and that is the owner's decision
rather than a derivation from contrast arithmetic.
The illustration is dark line-art over light fills drawn on a near-black
tile. A previous pass removed that tile from the SVG and replaced it with a
CSS plate that stayed light in both themes — the reasoning was sound (on a
dark page the ink collapses and a face is left floating) but the result was
not the drawing the owner made. The tile is back, byte-identical to
`content/assets/avatar.svg`, and the plate token it justified is gone.
So on the light theme this is a black square on pale chrome. That contrast
is intended: it is a printed object on the sheet, not a tint of it.
On dark the tile is near-black on near-black, so the EDGE is the only thing
left to say where the object stops — hence the stroke, which is a token with
a `dark` value rather than a theme query. `chrome-border-strong` measures
2.48:1 against the light head and 7.11:1 against the dark one, which is the
right way round: the theme that needs the edge gets the stronger one.
3.5rem because the drawing is 408 paths in an 80-unit box: at 40px its
features fall under a pixel and it reads as a smudge, at 56px it reads as a
face. The nav bar uses it far smaller and deliberately — see `.bar__face`,
where it is a mark rather than a portrait.
Round, like the one in the bar — see `.bar__face`. The drawing's own tile
is a rounded square and the circle crops its corners.

rules.name: body
note: The body is a FRAME, not a scroller. The surface inside it owns its own
scrolling, which is what keeps chat's defining property intact: its thread
is the bounded scroller and the composer stays pinned where a reader left
it. A scrolling body would take the composer with it.
The inset is `--space-5`, not `--pad`. `--pad` is the PAGE's inset and is
`clamp(1.25rem, 3vw, 3rem)` — it grows with the window because the well
grows with the window. The drawer's width stops at 46rem, so a viewport-fed
inset there is a tax that rises exactly when it buys nothing: at a 1440px
viewport it was taking 43px a side off a 736px panel, and the answer's own
components carry a second `--pad` inside that, so 21% of the panel was
margin. At `--space-5` the reading column is 696px.

rules.name: hosted-chat
note: ---- Hosting chat ----
Three rules, and each one only relaxes a bound that the PAGE needed and the
drawer supplies for free. `.chat__thread`'s `max-height: min(46rem, 75vh)`
exists so a growing conversation cannot stretch the band it sits in
(components/chat/spec.md). Here the sheet is `top: 0; bottom: 0` on a fixed
layer, so its height is the viewport and the thread cannot move it whatever
it contains — the bound is already structural, and keeping the max-height as
well would leave the composer floating in the middle of a tall panel.

rules.name: hosted-thread-empty
note: On the page an empty thread collapses so the composer is not preceded by an
empty box. In the drawer that row is the flexible one, so collapsing it
would let the composer stretch to the full height on first open.

rules.name: hosted-row
note: ---- Hosting the page's own components ----
`js/answer-render.js` renders answers as real `.idx__row`s, `.entry`s and
`.profile`s, and every one of those switches to a narrow layout at a
VIEWPORT breakpoint — which says nothing about the 736px column they are
actually in when a 1440px window has a drawer open. These restate the narrow
layout unconditionally inside the drawer. They are the rules a container
query would replace, and they are deliberately confined to the three
components whose wide layout actually breaks at this width.
The row's number stacks above the content at every width now (see the row
block), so the drawer's narrow restatement no longer carries a gutter —
just the main column and the chip, tags dropped as before.

rules.name: hosted-profile-pair
rules.$doc: A SCOPE, NOT AN APPEARANCE — the part that has no declarations and is the block that made them optional. The stylesheet writes `.drawer .profile > div:nth-child(odd)` and never `.drawer .profile > div`, because the only thing the drawer says about a hosted pair is what it says about the LEFT-hand ones: the gutter between two columns has nothing to be between once the grid is one column. Emitting an empty rule for the wrapper would claim a decision that was never made.

note: Same call `.sec__note` makes at 640px: the subtitle is chrome, and on a
phone it wraps to two lines and pushes the title off its own baseline.
